summary: This memo outlines high-level requirements for adding Mandatory Access Control to NFSv4.2. It describes the protections to be offered over protocol components and the basic structure of the proposed system.

plainLanguage.summary: Mandatory access control works by putting a security label on every file and every process, then comparing them. NFS breaks that model, because the files are on one machine and the processes on another. This RFC lists what NFS has to add so labels travel, are understood on both sides, and are enforced.

questions: what is a label format specifier
what are the labeled nfs modes
subtitle: What a network file system has to do so that mandatory access control still works across the network.

tldr.problem: Mandatory access control decides access by comparing a label on the subject with a label on the object. Over NFS, the object lives on a server and the subject runs on a client, so the labels have to travel and both ends have to agree on what they mean.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out the requirements: clients must convey their privileges, servers must store and return labels and notify of changes, and both must be able to negotiate and translate label formats. Labels carry a Label Format Specifier so that an opaque label can be interpreted, and three modes of operation are defined depending on which end enforces.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that records requirements rather than specifying a protocol. It also lists the trust assumptions that each mode needs, and warns that in Guest Mode one side is not enforcing anything at all.

today: RFC 7204 is an Informational RFC published in April 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a statement of requirements for Labeled NFS rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: Mandatory and Discretionary Access Control
sections.content:
Mandatory access control systems, as defined in the Internet Security Glossary, have been mainstreamed in modern operating systems such as Linux, FreeBSD and Solaris. They bind security attributes to subjects, which are processes, and to objects within the system, and those attributes are used with other information to make access control decisions.

Access control models such as Unix permissions or access control lists are commonly called discretionary access control. Those base their decisions on user identity and resource ownership. Mandatory models base their decisions on the label on the subject and on the object it wishes to reach. The labels may carry user identity information but usually carry more. In a discretionary system users are free to specify the access rules for the resources they own; a mandatory model bases its decisions on a system-wide policy that the users cannot override.

The RFC sets out the trade-off. Discretionary systems give some protection against unauthorized users running malicious software, but even an authorized user can execute malicious or flawed software with the program running at the full permissions of that user. Mandatory models can confine malicious or flawed software, and they usually act at a finer granularity than their discretionary counterparts.

Besides describing the requirements, the document records the functional requirements the client inherits from the security models already present on it. It says this may help readers outside the NFS community understand those issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Discretionary control lets a file's owner decide who may open it. Mandatory control puts the decision in a system-wide policy that the owner cannot overrule, and that is what lets a system contain broken or hostile software.

sections.title: The Terms Used
sections.content:
The definitions carry most of the requirements, so they are worth stating precisely.

An object is a passive resource the system wants to protect: files, directories, pipes, sockets and many other system resources relevant to the protection of the system state. A subject is an active entity, usually a process, requesting access to an object.

Labels come in two flavours. A foreign label is a label in a format other than the one the local mandatory access control implementation uses for encoding. A Label Format Specifier is an identifier the client uses to establish the syntactic format of the security label and the semantic meaning of its components. An optional part of a Label Format Specifier is the Policy Identifier, which lets clients and servers identify specific security policies.

Two capability levels are defined for servers and clients. A server is MAC-Aware if it can transmit and store object labels. A client or server is MAC-Functional if it is Labeled NFS enabled, meaning it can interpret labels and apply policies based on the security system. Multi-Level Security is the traditional model in which objects are given a sensitivity level, such as Unclassified, Secret or Top Secret, and a category set.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that can only carry labels around is MAC-Aware. One that can read them and act on them is MAC-Functional. The Label Format Specifier is the tag that says how to read the label that follows it.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements were gathered from users and developers and from earlier work in the area, such as the Distributed Trusted Operating System and the NSA's experimental NFSv3 enhancements.

The general requirements are four. Clients must be able to convey to the server the client's privileges, that is the subject making the request, so that the server may enforce a policy based on them. Servers must be able to store and retrieve the security attribute of exported files as the client requests. Servers must provide a mechanism for notifying clients of attribute changes of files. And clients and servers must be able to negotiate label formats and provide a mechanism to translate between them.

On security services, Labeled NFS or the system underneath it must provide authentication, integrity and privacy for all NFSv4.2 messaging, with the mechanisms configurable so that the level of protection can be set per mandatory security policy. Strong mutual authentication is required between server and client for Full Mode. Security labels and related state must always be protected by those services when they cross the network, as must the binding of labels and state to the objects and subjects they belong to.

On encoding, the encoding of labels and attributes passed over the network must be specified in a complete and unambiguous way while keeping the flexibility of the implementations. To do that, the labels must consist of a format-specific component bound with a Label Format Specifier, which identifies the structure and semantics of the opaque component, while the opaque component is the label the models will interpret. Because a given model requires a label to mean exactly the same thing on every system, it is recommended that most label formats incorporate semantically coherent labelling. Labeled NFS must provide a means for servers and clients to identify their Label Format Specifiers, and their mode of operation, and a negotiation scheme should let systems of different label formats agree how they will interpret or translate each other's foreign labels, with several concurrent agreements possible between a server and a client. All labels transferred across the network must be tagged with a valid Label Format Specifier, and a system that receives a label tagged with a specifier it does not recognise or cannot interpret must reject it.

On labelling, implementations must validate the labels supplied over the network against the set permitted from a specific peer and reject those that are not. At the client, labelling semantics for mounted file systems must stay consistent with those for locally mounted ones, with user-level labelling operations enacted locally through existing APIs. When an object is created by the client, the client calculates its label from its policy and sends the request, and the server may deny the creation with that label, and the server must bind the label to the object before the object becomes visible. The server must let clients retrieve security labels on all exported objects where possible, must honour a client-specified label on creation, and may reject it, and may translate a label but must not change its meaning.

On enforcement, a MAC-Functional client applies its own policy to remotely located objects using the labels it got from the server, and it must be possible to configure how long it may cache label state before revalidating it. If the server's policy changes, the client must flush all object state back to the server, and the server must check that flushed state against current policy before committing it. A MAC-Functional server must enforce its policy over all exported objects for operations that originate both locally and remotely, processing requests from authenticated clients using the labels and credentials the client supplied as if they had originated locally. The server should also recall a delegation when an object's label changes. The server should provide a way to authorize selective access to the exported namespace based on client credentials and policy, which is a common requirement of multi-level security systems that present selective views of namespaces based on subject clearances.
sections.plainLanguage: The client must say who is asking, the server must keep and return the labels and say when they change, and both ends must agree on how to read a label. Each side then applies its own policy to what the other returned.

sections.title: Modes of Operation
sections.content:
A client and server interaction can be described by three modes, which arise from the level of mandatory access control functionality on each side. Clients can be non-MAC-Functional or MAC-Functional; servers can be non-MAC-Functional, MAC-Aware or MAC-Functional. A MAC-Functional client must be able to determine the level of functionality in the server, and a MAC-Functional server must be able to determine whether the client is MAC-Functional, and the protocol must provide for both determinations.

In Full Mode the server and client have mutually recognized mandatory access control functionality enabled and full Labeled NFS functionality is extended over the network. On the initial lookup the client requests access to an object and sends its process security context; the server checks its policies to see whether that process context from that client may reach the resource, and if so releases the object with its security information; the client then applies its own policy. On later operations, where the client already has a handle, the order is reversed: the client checks its own policy first, which saves it sending requests that would fail anyway, and then sends the request so the server can apply its policy using the client's process context. A client that does not trust the server may use an alternate labelling mechanism regardless of the server's ability to return security information.

In Limited Server Mode the server is MAC-Aware and the clients are MAC-Functional. The server can store and transmit labels but cannot enforce them, and it must inform clients when an object label changes for a file the client has open. The server may not know the format of any of its object labels and may service several different security models at once, so the client must handle foreign labels. As with Guest Mode, this mode's level of trust can be degraded if non-MAC-Functional clients can reach the server.

In Guest Mode only one of the server or client is MAC-Functional. If the server is the enforcing side, it applies its policy and may selectively provide standard NFS services to clients based on their authentication credentials or associated network attributes, such as IP address or network interface. If the client is the enforcing side, it must operate as a standard NFSv4.2 client and should selectively give processes access to servers according to policy, and it may override the default labelling of the remote file system. In both cases the wire protocol is standard NFSv4.2, and the enforcing side maps the other side's processes or objects onto security labels so that its own guarantees hold.
sections.plainLanguage: Three arrangements: both ends enforce, only the server stores labels and only the client enforces, or only one end enforces while the other is a guest. The protocol must let each side work out which arrangement it is in.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples of how NFSv4.2 could be deployed in existing situations, and they are not meant to be exhaustive.

The first is full mandatory access control for remotely mounted file systems, in a local network where servers and clients are under common administration and all systems run the same implementation with semantically identical labels. An example is user home directories mounted remotely, where fine-grained policy protects private user data from being read by malicious web scripts running in the user's browser, which labelled NFS makes possible.

The second is labelling virtual machine images stored on the network. Guest file systems are commonly stored on a networked server and mounted by the guest at instantiation, and the guest kernel needs to read fine-grained labels on that file system so that its own policy applies.

The third is simple security label storage, in a mixed and loosely administered network where nodes run different operating systems with different security mechanisms. Here the file servers are simply able to store and return labels, and the protocol is implemented only to carry labels across the network. The RFC notes that overall security cannot be enforced as strongly in such an environment as when the server is also enforcing, and that the aim is to let MAC-capable clients keep their policy switched on rather than disable it.

The fourth is diskless Linux, where a distribution depends on a mandatory access control model to implement a kernel-enforced policy that assigns roles to processes and limits what they may do to files, directories, sockets and other objects. Enforcement is typically a matter for the diskless client itself, so using RPCSEC_GSSv3 to enforce compliance at the server is of limited value. Being able to label files permanently and have those labels read back by the client is what makes such policies work, including role transitions that standard NFS access control models cannot replicate.

The fifth is multi-level security, where objects get a sensitivity level and a set of compartments, and read access is allowed when the subject's level dominates the object's and its compartments are a superset. The example uses Unclassified, Secret and Top Secret levels and a directory labelled Top Secret, so only a Top Secret subject may read it. With a MAC-Functional client and server, a process running at Secret that calls readdir() is stopped by the client's MAC module before any request leaves the machine, while a process running at Top Secret passes, sends the request with the right credential, and the server checks its own module before returning the contents. If the two ends run different policies, a translation of the labels might be needed, and a check could pass on the client and fail on the server: a server that treats a subnet as cleared only up to Secret would refuse a client asserting Top Secret on it.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC shows labels being used for remote home directories, for virtual machine images, as a simple store of labels on a mixed network, for diskless clients with role-based policies, and for classified networks where a clearance decides what can be read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Labeled NFS is a transport mechanism for labels, a storage requirement for labels, and a definition of how to interpret labels. It defines the responsibilities of client and server in the various permutations of being MAC-Functional, but it does not dictate whether assumptions can be made about other entities in the relationship. For example, it does not define whether a MAC-Functional client can demand that a MAC-Aware server accept requests only from other MAC-Functional clients. That is a policy based on a mandatory access control model, and the document does not impose policies on systems. Because the requirement is a policy, it can be met with the model itself: a new Label Format Specifier can be created that adds the rule that the MAC-Aware server must not accept any requests from a non-MAC-Functional client.

In Guest Mode one side is not enforcing mandatory access control protections. Alternate methods are used to handle the lack of support, and care should be taken to identify and mitigate threats from possible tampering outside those methods.

The third point is about the client's own configuration. If the process labels are created solely on the client, then a malicious user with sufficient access on that client compromises the model. This is no different from current implementations in which the server uses policies to determine the object label for requests from the client, or from local decisions made by the client's own security system. Either the server must explicitly trust the client, or the model must enforce that users cannot override the policies, perhaps through an externally managed source. Once the labels leave the client, the transport mechanism described in the requirements protects them.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not decide who to trust. That is a policy choice for each deployment. What it does warn about is Guest Mode, where one side enforces nothing, and a client that creates its own labels, where a user with enough access to that client can break the whole scheme.

viz.caption: THE TERMS THE REQUIREMENTS TURN ON

items.title: Label Format Specifier
items.text: An identifier the client uses to establish the syntax of a security label and the meaning of its components.

items.title: Foreign label
items.text: A label in a format other than the one the local mandatory access control implementation uses.

items.title: MAC-Aware
items.text: A server that can transmit and store object labels.

items.title: MAC-Functional
items.text: A client or server that can interpret labels and apply policies based on the security system.

items.title: Policy Identifier
items.text: An optional part of a Label Format Specifier that lets clients and servers name a specific security policy.
